summary: For ages 5–7: water can be solid (ice and snow) or liquid; snow is made of countless tiny frozen ice crystals; icebergs are huge chunks of ice floating in the ocean with most of their bulk hidden underwater; and ice floats because frozen water is lighter than the same amount of liquid water (not because of size or weight). Teach it observationally and hands-on, building intuition through predict-then-check with real floating ice, and seed the memorable 'tip of the iceberg' picture. A screen model where a child tries to push a floating cube under is a strong scaffold, but real materials deliver the felt surprise most directly.
misconceptions: Ice is a different substance from water — it is the same water, just frozen solid
All heavy things sink, so a giant iceberg should sink — ice floats no matter how big because it is lighter than water
An iceberg is all above the water you can see — most of it is hidden underwater
Snow is like white sand or cotton — it is made of tiny frozen ice crystals
Melting destroys the water — melting just turns solid ice back into liquid water

activities.title: Push the ice under — and watch it bob back
steps: Get a real ice cube or chunk and a clear cup or tub of water ready.
Before placing the ice in the water, PREDICT out loud whether the big, heavy ice will sink or float, and say WHY first.
Place it in the water and OBSERVE: it floats with only a small part sticking up.
Mark the waterline on the clear cup so you can see how much sits BELOW the surface versus the little tip above.
Try to push the ice all the way under and hold it there, then let go and watch it bob back up every time.
Say in your own words: most of the ice is hidden underwater, and it floats because ice is lighter than the same amount of water — not because of how big it is.
activities.insight: Ice floats because frozen water is lighter than the same amount of liquid water; size and weight do not decide it, and most of a floating chunk (like an iceberg) is hidden below the surface.

activities.title: Melt it, freeze it — same water
steps: Hold a little ice or snow in a warm hand and watch it turn to water.
Talk about how the puddle is the SAME water, just no longer frozen.
Place liquid water somewhere cold (or imagine the freezer) and describe how it would turn back to solid ice.
Match a picture pair or sequence: ice → melting puddle → refrozen ice, saying which is solid and which is liquid each time.
activities.insight: Ice and snow are frozen water (solid); melting turns the solid back into liquid water, and freezing turns liquid back into solid — the water itself is not destroyed or changed into a different substance.

activities.title: What is snow made of?
steps: Look closely at real snowflakes, or at magnified snowflake photographs.
Describe the tiny crystal shapes you can see.
Explain that snow is not like white sand or cotton — it is made of countless tiny frozen ice crystals.
Hold a little snow in a warm hand and watch it melt to water, confirming it is frozen water too.
activities.insight: Snow is made of many tiny frozen ice crystals — it is frozen water, not a fluffy material like cotton or sand.

activities.title: The hidden iceberg (diagnostic discussion)
steps: Look at a picture or cross-section of a huge iceberg floating with a little poking up above the water.
Respond to a friend's claim: 'Something that big and heavy should sink — and what you see poking up is pretty much the whole thing.'
Say whether the friend is right that it should sink, and whether the bit above water is most of the iceberg or just a little — and explain how you know.
Discuss: Why does a giant iceberg float when a small pebble sinks — is it about size? If most of the iceberg is underwater, why might that be dangerous for a ship?
activities.insight: A huge, heavy iceberg floats because ice is lighter than the same amount of liquid water (size is irrelevant), and the visible tip is only a small part — most is hidden underwater.

checkQuestion: Here is a huge, heavy iceberg floating in the sea, with a little poking up above the water. A friend says 'something that big and heavy should sink — and what you see poking up is pretty much the whole thing.' Is your friend right that it should sink? And is the bit above the water most of the iceberg, or just a little of it — how do you know?
checkAnswer: The friend is wrong on both counts. A big heavy iceberg FLOATS because ice is lighter than the same amount of liquid water (frozen water takes up more room, so it floats) — size doesn't decide it. And the part poking up is only a SMALL part; MOST of the iceberg is hidden underwater. Ice and snow are just frozen water (solid), which can melt back to liquid.
